Review Date: Reviewed in the United States on February 17, 2025
Review Body: The main topic of the book - increase in screen time and social media leads to anxiety and other mental health issues for kids - is something society recognizes and agrees on (for the most part). The statistics are interesting and alarming. Overall it is an intro book perhaps for the general population? As an educator it felt a little oversimplified, repetitive, and not exactly full of new epiphanies for me personally. It is not a bad book by any means, I just didn't feel I learned a ton of new information from it, which is what I had hoped for.

Review Date: Reviewed in the United States on February 15, 2025
Review Body:
I bought this book hoping to find answers. There were 3 pages on what parents should do for teenagers which I already knew (e.g. "get a job"). I was hoping for more suggestions than the obvious. The rest of the 300 pages were data to show there's a problem and help explain why and implications.

Great to know I'm not alone, but I ended up skipping all but a couple of chapters. I know there's a problem with screens, games and social media. It's pretty obvious why this is all additive and how it's screwing up our kids. Kids get to a certain age, and it becomes a lot harder to be strict. All parents would need to throw their kid's devices away and major tech companies would need to think of what's best for humanity vs profits... that will never happen.

3 stars is for the research, but I didn't find the book helped me at all.

Review Date: Reviewed in the United States on December 22, 2024
Review Body:
This book sparked my interest in reading the discussions around whether the use of social media has an impact of greater incidences of mental illness. It is worth reading this book, as well as critical reviews of it.

I was interested to read about the authors’ views on how girls and boys use the Internet differently.

I appreciated the author’s overall point that parents are overprotective in the real physical world but under protective in the virtual world, especially social media.

As a millennial parent these are immortal issues I need to consider and it was helpful to learn about the concrete suggestions the author proposed, including when to allow children of different ages access to the Internet, phones, opening of accounts on social media platforms, use of tracking devices by parents of their children etc. Of course, there is no one size fits all and it is important to reflect on these issues in your child’s specific circumstances.

This book appears mainly to be based on US and some European data.

Review Date: Reviewed in the United States on December 10, 2024
Review Body:
Haidt has written another pop psychology polemic. There is little in the way of causation vs correlation to explain the increase in anomie, identity crisis and overall distress among GenZ. There are some useful insights that are not prioritized such as the decline in the concept of children's play which almost universally included fantasy role playing, identifying with historic figures like cowboys, conquering aliens, comic book superheroes,GI Joe, nurses, etc. The emotional connection between playful fantasy and social interaction during childhood and early adolescence binding children together in face-to-face shared identities, is being lost. Boys playing sports in their neighborhood after school taught valuable lessons about competition and cooperation. This is emblematic in the Peanut's cartoon where Charlie Brown is playing baseball and is thinking of stealing home (competitive) but thinks that if he is tagged out he'll be the goat (cooperative) and in his dilemma leading off third base he is tagged out.
Childhood play involves fantasy and imagination. Today's computer games present graphic images and rely far more on eye-hand and muscle coordination than fantasy and imagination--the images are all too graphic. Computer games are played primarily in social isolation against cyber players. This is a serious fragmentation between fantasy, role playing, emotional intelligence and a sense of self.  

There were efforts to examine children's play post World War II beginning in the 1950s. This led to an examination of the relationship of death to childhood and the emergence of sexuality. Where death was once ever present in a child's environment and sexuality a fantasy it reversed with the role of hospitals for those aging and infirm and the absence of the familiar family home death scene where children were present. With the rise of hospitals, death was anesthetized and became fantasy for children and now sexual imagery became normative. By the 1990s graphicly illustrated computer games replaced both death and sexual fantasies where body dismembering and explosions and violence now became reality leaving nothing to the imagination; how violence  even sexuual violence is now an INDIVIDUAL not a collective construct. It is a reality not shared by immediate friends but abstract "friends" on the web. Even mom's role organizing children's play is transformed: giving this role to machine organized virtual play dates. The cycle is complete and children are now fully disconnected from face-to-face interactions to isolation and the vicissitudes of social media fragmentation. The longed for global community made possible by global technology nnow replaces how  by major events such as the civil rights movement, the threat of the nuclear arms race and the antiwar movement all of which required face-to-face social interaction and community has now given way to cell phone revolutions like Arab Spring, that quickly fell apart because it lacked face-to-face social cohesiveness.

I am rambling, but my point is that we never had guardrails when it came to the internet as we did before where the limitations of a global community were more difficult to achieve. In the process of creating the world wide web within a decade, there was little time to understand and limit its control over every facet of childhood development. Finally, we are also bearing witness to the impact of the dual worker household and the rise of latch key kids--further childhood and adolescence  fragmentation.

There is so much more that Haight never gets too that makes his analysis both empty and at the same time a number one best seller. This tells you all you need to know about the diminution of critical thinking and its relacement with unsupported opinions as public "fact" all over the internet. The concept of "fake news" is part of this  important, dramatic shift from trusted long term relationships with media to fragments in cyberspace where everything is both real and imaginary 24/7--the conundrum is at any given moment, which one is it?

Review Date: Reviewed in the United States on October 17, 2024
Review Body:
I 100% agree that being online & having smartphones before high school is a no go. But the author alludes to phone/net use causing kids brains to be developed into seeing the world as dangerous rather than safe. That happens w/in the first 3-5 years, and is from parental neglect, not online use. I’m studying child development that fact thrown in there bothered me.

The author also seriously downplays the sexual assault accusations of children toward adults, particularly Cub Scout leaders.. “it came out that the children made up a story.” Yes, this happens sometimes, but kids don’t made up SA allegations for fun, it’s coming from somewhere. He pokes fun, in a way, at parents wanting to protect their kids from sexual assault and kidnapping, and says it’s less common now than it used to be. How does that fare sitting next to the “1 in 4 kids will be sexually assaulted by age 16” statistic? And next to all of us adults who were not kept safe by our parents during childhood, and were therefore subjected to sexual assault, and a lifetime of PTSD as a result?

Author also stresses some importance in peer orientation in late childhood & teen years. And while yes! Independence is great for kids, I also read “Hold Onto Your Kids” by Dr. Gabor Matè, which stresses how peer orientation will seriously mess your kids up.

I agree, no phones or social media for kids. But it feels like this author is grabbing at some straws to drive his point home, when it’s not even necessary. Less than halfway through, and I’m of the mind “Okay, I get it. No phones or social media for kids. I think I can be done listening to this now…” but there’s 7.5 hours left.

I’m an adult, and can cherry pick from this book what is useful and what is not, and so can you! But I can see how a parent who gives their kid free reign over an iPad/ smartphone/youtube/internet requires 9 hours and a little exaggeration, to be convinced that it’s a bad parenting choice.

Review Date: Reviewed in the United States on June 29, 2024
Review Body:
At p.34 of Haidt's book he cites MIT professor Sherry Turkle's observation that due to the ubiquity of Internet use (no doubt exacerbated with the invention of smartphones), "We are forever elsewhere". An important point in this observation is that it applies to "we"; not just children and teens, but just about everybody in our 21st century culture. Haidt's book is o.k.; but it immediately struck me as rather disingenuous. It's like encouraging a bunch of alcoholics to get together in a bar to see what they can do about teen drinking.
As I see it, there is little doubt, that despite its advantages, the Internet has in certain fundamental ways, induced a near vacuum in the minds of people throughout society; and that the only real solution, is for just about everybody to use it a lot less and more judiciously.
I could cite a lot of books on this point, but in my opinion the best one is a book cited by Haidt himself at p.127 of his book,i.e., Nicholas Carr's "The Shallows: What the Internet Is Doing to Our Brains" (2010,2011). I would recommend reading Carr's book for a real sense of context before reading Haidt's book.

Review Date: Reviewed in the United States on April 17, 2024
Review Body:
I only made it through 15% of the book. It seems like it’s another book that has a straightforward thesis, but still spends hundreds of pages providing superfluous details and examples, probably to meet a page requirement / write a book rather than a blog post.

For this book, the thesis is effectively that social media is bad and causes mental health problems. I think we all know this. It’s not a novel take. I do appreciate that it takes a scientific approach and seeks to provide copious amounts of data, but I think comprehending the thesis and moving on with your life probably would be the best approach.
